sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Verification load tests on pre-production micropiles verify bond zone strength assumptions and the contractor's installation methods, usually as the first order of work; production micropiles are approved only after that. Proof tests on selected production micropiles confirm installation procedures (quality assurance). Tests follow conventional static procedures for driven piles and drilled shafts, loading incrementally (compression, tension or lateral, possibly cycled) to a maximum test load, displacement limit or creep threshold.
sections.body: (p. 7-1) On micropile foundation support and slope stabilization projects, 'verification' load testing is performed on pre-production micropiles to verify design assumptions about bond zone strength and the adequacy of the contractor's installation methods. It is usually the first order of work under the construction contract, and production micropiles are approved only after these have been verified; on large projects additional load testing may be performed during design under a separate contract. The ability of the micropile to safely carry the design load in service is obtained through 'proof' load testing on selected production micropiles, a quality assurance means to confirm installation procedures. Micropiles are tested individually with the same conventional static load testing procedures as driven piles and drilled shafts: incremental loading (in compression, tension or laterally, and possibly cycled, i.e., load/unload) until the micropile reaches the selected maximum test load, structural displacement limit, or ground creep (movement under constant load) threshold. The chapter describes verification and proof tests, typical equipment, load increment schedules and analysis of load-deformation data used to judge acceptance for payment.

sections.title: Overview of Micropile Load Testing
sections.summary: Load tests verify design loads are carried without excessive movement and with adequate factor of safety, and check drilling, installation and grouting before (verification) and during (proof) production; production installation must match the test micropiles. Verification tests load to the bond factor of safety; ultimate tests to failure (research or very large projects). One or two verification tests are common, more per ground type. Proof tests are on production piles; creep tests are part of both.
sections.body: (pp. 7-1 to 7-2) Micropiles are load tested to verify that the required design loads can be carried without excessive movement and with an adequate factor of safety for the life of the structure, and to verify the contractor's drilling, installation and grouting before (verification testing) and during (proof testing) production. Ground conditions and the method, equipment and operator for production piles must therefore be similar to those for the test micropiles; if ground or installation procedures change, additional testing should be required. If results indicate faulty construction or grout-to-ground capacities less than required, the contractor may be required to modify installation methods, and if the required bond capacities are still not achievable, redesign may be necessary. Specifications typically include ultimate and/or verification tests: loading to a maximum test load that includes the factor of safety on the design grout-to-ground bond (verification test) and/or to failure, defined as the inability to maintain constant test load without excessive movement (ultimate test). Ultimate tests are usually specified only for research or very large projects where a design phase test program, which allows the design to be optimized, can be justified. On typical projects one or two verification tests are commonly conducted before production installation, and one or more more may be conducted in each significantly different ground type as construction proceeds; larger projects may specify more (minimum number in Section 7.6.2). Since ultimate and verification tests reach relatively high loads, these micropiles are often 'sacrificial'. During production, 'proof' tests are conducted on a specified number of production piles, which are incorporated into the structure provided the test loads are below those causing geotechnical or structural failure or damage (minimum numbers in Section 7.6.3). Creep tests, similar to those for ground anchors and soil nails, are part of verification and proof tests: movement is measured at constant load over a specified time to assess whether design loads can be carried throughout the service life; creep is primarily a concern in organic soils and in cohesive soils with liquid limit greater than 50 and plasticity index greater than 20.
key_points: Load tests verify design loads are carried without excessive movement and with adequate factor of safety for the structure's life
Production piles must use ground, method, equipment and operator similar to the test micropiles; changes call for more testing
Poor results may require modified installation methods or, if bond capacity is still not achieved, redesign
Verification test: maximum load includes the factor of safety on the design grout-to-ground bond
Ultimate test: to failure (cannot hold constant load without excessive movement); research or very large projects
Typically one or two verification tests before production, plus more in significantly different ground; test piles are often sacrificial
Proof tests on production piles that stay in the structure if loads stay below failure and damage
Creep tests are part of verification and proof tests; creep matters mainly in organic soils and clays with LL > 50 and PI > 20

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Micropiles are tested with the same equipment and methods as driven piles and drilled shafts: ASTM D 1143 (compression), ASTM D 3689 (tension) and ASTM D 3966 (lateral); typical setups are in Figures 7-1 to 7-3. Equipment: hydraulic jack and pump; reaction and reference beams; pressure gauges and load cells; dial gauges; wire with mirror and scale.
sections.body: (p. 7-3) The equipment and load testing methods used for micropiles are the same as those for conventional load testing of driven piles and drilled shafts, as codified in ASTM D 1143 for compression loading, ASTM D 3689 for tension loading and ASTM D 3966 for lateral loading. Typical compression, tension and lateral setups are shown in Figures 7-1, 7-2 and 7-3. Typical load testing equipment includes: (1) hydraulic jack and pump; (2) reaction and reference beams; (3) pressure gauges and load cells; (4) dial gauges; and (5) wire with mirror and scale.

sections.title: Load Testing Equipment
sections.summary: Loads are applied by a hydraulic jack against a reaction: a beam anchored by piles, micropiles or ground anchors, or a weighted platform (compression, Figure 7-4); a reaction frame on the test pile (tension, Figure 7-5); or between two piles (lateral, Figure 7-6). Pressure gauges give load; calibrate within 45 working days (Figure 7-7), keep a master gauge. Load cells hold constant load; not required for proof tests. Dial gauges read to 0.025 mm, at least 2.13 m from the pile, three averaged.
sections.body: (pp. 7-3 to 7-10) The most common system is a hydraulic jack and reaction arrangement. For compression, the load is applied by jacking against a beam anchored by piles, micropiles or ground anchors (Figure 7-4), or against a weighted platform. For tension, the jack is centered on a test beam (possibly supported on cribbing) and jacks against a reaction frame connected to the test micropile (Figure 7-5). For lateral tests, a jack acts against a reaction system or between two piles (Figure 7-6), allowing two lateral tests simultaneously. The standard load monitor is a pressure gauge on the jack pump, used for the absolute value of applied load; pressure gauges should be calibrated within 45 working days of the date they are submitted for approval, calibration certifications and graphs for gauges and load cells must be provided before use (example curve, Figure 7-7), and a second certified 'master' gauge should be kept on site to check the jack gauges. Calibrated load cells should be used to verify that load stays constant during the hold periods of an ultimate (and/or verification) test; they must be aligned with the axis of the micropile and jack, and are used mainly to detect small load changes so that a constant holding load is maintained (e.g., keeping a reading of '440' through jack pressure adjustments for the whole creep test). Load cells are not required for proof tests (except extended creep testing to judge acceptability). Head movement is measured with dial gauges and/or LVDTs on the reference beams, read to the nearest 0.025 mm (0.001 in); for axial tests the independent reference beam's supports are at five times the test micropile diameter, the minimum distance between gauges and test micropile is 2.13 m (7 ft) (Figures 7-1, 7-2), and three gauges placed equidistant around the pile are averaged to compensate for head rotation. A mirror and scale on the pile with a wire strung on a separate reference is a less sensitive backup only. Telltales (metal or fiberglass rods anchored in the grout, sheathed above) can measure axial displacement at discrete elevations, protected from damage by drill string rotation or grout in the sheath. Strain gauges (vibrating-wire type recommended) on the reinforcing steel give axial load distribution with depth, and diametrically opposite pairs on the casing give bending moments with depth (Figure 7-8). For lateral tests, an inclinometer installed to 10 to 20 micropile diameters (depth from the design lateral analyses) is recommended.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Verification loads can be applied in compression, tension or laterally. The maximum compression or tension test load is typically set by the grout-to-ground bond factor of safety used in design, usually 2.0 to 2.5 times the design axial load; lateral tests go to 2.0 times the design lateral load. Acceptance criteria are in Section 7.4.3.
sections.body: (p. 7-11) For verification tests, loads can be applied in compression, tension or laterally. The maximum test load for a compression or tension test is typically defined by the grout-to-ground bond factor of safety used in design; for micropiles the maximum verification test load will usually be 2.0 to 2.5 times the design axial (compression or tension) load. Lateral load tests are performed to 2.0 times the design lateral load. Acceptance criteria based on load test results are provided in Section 7.4.3.

Maximum axial test load set by the design grout-to-ground bond factor of safety: usually 2.0 to 2.5 times the design axial load
Lateral verification tests to 2.0 times the design lateral load

sections.title: Procedures for Verification Test
sections.summary: The micropile is loaded and unloaded incrementally, reading head movement just after each load and again once stable, per the first three columns of Table 7-1 (DFI, 2004). An alignment load (AL, no more than 10 percent of design load) zeroes the gauges; cycles return to AL and rise to the test load. A hold of ten minutes (movement at 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10 minutes; load within 0.35 MPa) is the creep test, extended 50 minutes if creep exceeds the maximum.
sections.body: (p. 7-11) Verification testing incrementally loads and unloads the micropile and measures head movement at each increment, with a reading just after the load is applied and a second after the load has been held long enough for movement to stabilize. The load schedule is the first three columns of Table 7-1, consistent with DFI (2004). The first step applies a nominal alignment load (AL), typically no more than ten percent of the design load, to ensure the stressing and testing equipment are aligned; the displacement equipment is zeroed when the AL stabilizes (Figure 7-9). In the first cycle the load is raised to 15 percent of the design load (as printed) and the incremental movement recorded, then reduced back to the alignment load; this is repeated with the increments of Table 7-1 until the maximum test load is reached. At the test load a constant load is held for ten minutes before unloading; the load is taken as reasonably constant if the deviation from the test pressure does not exceed 0.35 MPa (50 psi). During the hold, movements are recorded at 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10 minutes to measure time-dependent (creep) movement; this portion is the creep test. If the total movement between 1 and 10 minutes exceeds the specified maximum creep movement, the load is held another 50 minutes and total movement recorded at 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 minutes.
key_points: Load and unload incrementally; read head movement just after each load and again when stable
Load schedule: first three columns of Table 7-1, consistent with DFI (2004)
Alignment load AL, no more than 10 percent of design load, zeroes the gauges (Figure 7-9)
Each cycle returns to AL; increments per Table 7-1 up to the test load
Creep hold of ten minutes with readings at 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10 minutes; load within 0.35 MPa (50 psi) of the test pressure
If movement between 1 and 10 minutes exceeds the maximum, hold 50 minutes more and read at 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 minutes

sections.title: Recording of Verification Test Data
sections.summary: Load comes from the jack pressure gauge and load cell. Total movement (delta t) at each increment and at AL is split into residual movement (delta r, the irrecoverable movement on return to AL, including elongation and movement through the ground) and elastic movement (total at the cycle maximum minus the AL reading) (Figures 7-9, 7-10, Table 7-1). Residual movement is not used for acceptance but indicates bond zone behavior. Creep starts when 1.30 DL is applied: 1 to 10 minutes, or 6 to 60 minutes if extended.
sections.body: (pp. 7-12 to 7-14) The magnitude of each load is determined from the jack pressure gauge and the load cell. The load-deformation data for each increment are plotted as in Figure 7-10. The total movement (delta t) is recorded at each load increment and at the alignment load; it consists of elastic and residual movement. The residual movement for an increment is the net 'irrecoverable' movement after applying the increment and reducing the load to the alignment load (Figure 7-9, delta r4); it includes elongation of the micropile and movement of the entire micropile through the ground. Elastic movement is the arithmetic difference between the total movement at the maximum load of a cycle and the movement at the alignment load (Table 7-1). Residual movement is not used for acceptance, but indicates the stress-strain behavior of the ground-to-grout bond in the bond zone and should be collected for future testing or design in similar ground and loads. During the creep test, movements at 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10 minutes are recorded; the time at which 1.30 DL is applied (Figure 7-9) is the start time, and the movement from one to ten minutes after it is compared with the creep acceptance criterion. If the criterion is not satisfied, the load is held an additional 50 minutes and the total movement between 6 and 60 minutes is compared with the specified criteria.
key_points: Load from the jack pressure gauge and the load cell
Total movement = elastic + residual; residual is the irrecoverable movement on return to the alignment load (Figure 7-9)
Elastic movement = total movement at the cycle maximum minus the movement at the alignment load (Table 7-1)
Residual movement is not an acceptance criterion but shows bond zone behavior; keep it for future design in similar ground
Creep start time is when 1.30 DL is applied; compare 1-10 minute movement with the criterion, or 6-60 minute movement if extended
Table 7-1 cycles: 0.15-0.45 DL; 0.15-1.00 DL; 0.15-1.45 DL with creep hold at 1.30 DL; 0.15-2.00 DL (10 min hold) then unload in steps to AL

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Proof tests are run during construction on a percentage of production micropiles to verify that the construction procedure has stayed the same and that micropiles were not drilled and grouted in a soil zone the verification tests did not cover. Micropiles are proof tested to a load typically equal to 160 percent of the design load, in compression, tension or laterally.
sections.body: (p. 7-15) Proof tests are conducted during construction on a percentage of the total production micropiles installed. They are intended to verify that the contractor's construction procedure has remained constant and that the micropiles have not been drilled and grouted in a soil zone not tested by the verification testing. Micropiles are proof tested to a load typically equal to 160 percent of the design load; loads can be applied in compression, tension or laterally.
key_points: Proof tests during construction on a percentage of production micropiles
They verify the construction procedure has not changed and no untested soil zone has been used
Proof test load typically 160 percent of the design load, in compression, tension or laterally

sections.title: Proof Test Procedures and Recording and Analysis of Proof Test Data
sections.summary: The proof test follows the DFI (2004) schedule in Table 7-2: AL, then 0.15 DL steps to 1.30 DL (creep zero reading), a creep hold of at least 10 minutes (extended to 60 if needed), 1.45 and 1.60 DL, and unloading in steps to AL. Residual and elastic movements are calculated for the test load from the unload cycle, as for verification tests (Figure 7-11). Creep starts at 1.3 DL; creep movement is total movement minus the one-minute reading, and the 1-10 minute movement is compared with the criteria.
sections.body: (p. 7-15) The proof test loading schedule codified in DFI (2004) is outlined in Table 7-2, and results of an example proof test are plotted in Figure 7-11. The residual and elastic movements should be calculated for the test load from the unload cycle, as described for verification tests. During the creep test portion, movements at 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10 minutes are recorded; the time at which 1.3 DL is applied is the start time. The creep movement at any time is the difference between the total movement and the movement measured at one minute, and the creep rate is the slope of the curve per log cycle of time. The movement from one to ten minutes after the start is compared with the creep acceptance criteria.

sections.title: Acceptance of Verification Test
sections.summary: Three criteria (DFI, 2004): (1) rate of head movement at the test load: the slope of load versus head settlement must not exceed 0.15 mm/kN (0.025 in/kip) at 2.0 times the design load (failure load = where it first exceeds that; the Davisson criterion, used for driven piles and drilled shafts, has not been evaluated for micropiles); (2) total head movement at the design load, a project-specific limit; (3) creep at 1.3 DL: not more than 1 mm between 1 and 10 minutes, or else not more than 2 mm between 6 and 60 minutes.
sections.body: (pp. 7-15 to 7-18) There are three primary acceptance criteria for a verification-tested micropile. Rate of Pile Head Movement at the Test Load: acceptance includes assessing whether failure has occurred at the test load (e.g., 2.0 times the design load). A plunging failure is typically not reached at this load, so failure may be defined by the rate of head movement per unit load: acceptance requires that the slope of the load versus micropile head settlement curve be less than or equal to 0.15 mm/kN (0.025 in/kip) at 2.0 times the design load (DFI, 2004); restated, the failure load is where that slope first exceeds 0.15 mm/kN (0.025 in/kip). Driven piles and drilled shafts use the Davisson criterion to define the failure load, but it is difficult to use for micropiles because axial stiffness changes along the length (cased and uncased lengths), and its use for micropiles has not been evaluated. Total Pile Head Movement at the Design Load: a maximum head movement for a single micropile at the design load, for compression, tension or lateral tests, selected by the design engineer from the movements the supported superstructure can tolerate on a project-specific basis. Total Pile Head Movement under Sustained Load (Creep): the measured total movement during the required hold at 1.3 DL should not exceed 1 mm (0.04 in.) between 1 and 10 minutes; if it does, the load is held another 50 minutes, and the micropile is acceptable with respect to creep if the movement does not exceed 2 mm (0.08 in.) between 6 and 60 minutes.
key_points: Three criteria: rate of head movement at the test load, total head movement at the design load, and creep
Rate criterion: slope of load versus head settlement <= 0.15 mm/kN (0.025 in/kip) at 2.0 times the design load (DFI, 2004)
Failure load: where the load-settlement slope first exceeds 0.15 mm/kN; plunging failure is typically not reached
Davisson criterion (driven piles, drilled shafts) is hard to apply with cased and uncased lengths and has not been evaluated for micropiles
Total head movement at the design load: project-specific limit from the supported superstructure, for compression, tension or lateral tests
Creep at 1.3 DL: <= 1 mm (0.04 in.) between 1 and 10 minutes; otherwise hold 50 minutes more and accept if <= 2 mm (0.08 in.) between 6 and 60 minutes
sections.applicability: The three acceptance criteria for a verification-tested micropile: rate of movement at the test load, total movement at design load and creep.

sections.title: Acceptance of Proof Test
sections.summary: The verification criteria for total head movement at the design load and under sustained load (creep) apply to proof-tested micropiles. The creep test is performed at 1.3 DL (printed as 'the maximum test load which is typically 1.3 DL'; Table 7-2 continues to 1.60 DL), evaluated as for verification tests. The creep criteria very rarely govern acceptance of load-tested micropiles.
sections.body: (p. 7-18) The acceptance criteria for verification tests for total pile head movement at the design load and for total pile head movement under sustained load are used for a proof-tested micropile. For a proof-tested micropile, the creep test is performed at what the print calls the maximum test load, typically 1.3 DL (Table 7-2 and Section 7.4.2.1 take the proof test to 1.60 DL, with the creep hold at 1.30 DL). Acceptable creep movements are evaluated as for verification-tested micropiles. The creep criteria very rarely govern the acceptance of load-tested micropiles.
key_points: Proof tests use the verification criteria for total head movement at the design load and for creep
Proof test creep hold at 1.3 DL, judged as for verification tests
Creep criteria very rarely govern acceptance of load-tested micropiles
sections.applicability: Acceptance criteria applied to proof-tested micropiles.

sections.title: Consequences of Failure
sections.summary: If a verification micropile fails, the contractor can modify the micropile design and/or construction procedure: replacement micropiles, modified installation, longer bond length, regrouting through pre-placed tubes or a different micropile type, at the contractor's cost, with Owner review of any change to the structure. If a proof test fails, another nearby micropile is proof tested, and the design and/or procedure is modified for the failed and remaining micropiles (including reduced-capacity micropiles), at the contractor's expense.
sections.body: (pp. 7-18 to 7-19) If a micropile fails the acceptance criteria during verification testing of pre-production micropiles, the contractor can modify the design of the micropile and/or the construction procedure to provide the required capacity: installing replacement micropiles, modifying installation procedures, increasing the bond length, regrouting via pre-placed re-grout tubes, or changing the micropile type. Any modification requiring changes to the structure shall have prior review and acceptance by the Owner, and the cost of the changes should be incurred by the contractor. If failure occurs during proof testing of production piles, the contractor shall be directed to proof test another nearby micropile; for failed micropiles and further construction, the contractor shall modify the design, the construction procedure, or both: replacement micropiles, micropiles of reduced load capacity, modified installation methods, increased bond length, or a different micropile type. Any modification requiring changes to the structure shall have prior review and acceptance by the Owner and should be at the contractor's expense.
key_points: Verification failure: contractor may modify micropile design and/or construction procedure
Remedies: replacement micropiles, modified installation, longer bond length, regrouting via pre-placed tubes, different micropile type
Proof test failure: proof test another nearby micropile, then modify design and/or procedure (reduced-capacity micropiles are an option)
Changes to the structure need prior Owner review and acceptance; costs are the contractor's
sections.applicability: Remedies when a verification or proof test micropile fails acceptance.

sections.title: Micropile Load Test Report
sections.summary: A report for each load test goes to the Owner, typically within 24 to 48 hours of completion. Minimum contents: project description; site and subsurface conditions at the test location compared with those encountered; key personnel (drill rig operator, superintendent, grout plant operator); installation data (cased and uncased lengths, bags of cement, casing and reinforcement, geology, drilling and grouting records); results with data sheets and figures; requirements and acceptance criteria and their comparison; summary; gauge and load cell calibrations; material certifications.
sections.body: (p. 7-19) For each load test, a report must be written and submitted to the Owner, typically within 24 to 48 hours of completion. It should include at least: a brief project description; site and subsurface conditions, including ground conditions at the test location and a comparison with actual conditions encountered; key personnel, including the drill rig operator, superintendent, grout plant operator and others involved in installing and testing the micropile; installation data, such as length (cased and uncased), number of bags of cement used, size and type of casing and reinforcement, geology encountered (soil, rock, water levels) and actual drilling and grouting records; load test results, including filled-out data sheets and data presentation figures; a statement of load test requirements and acceptance criteria; a comparison of the requirements and acceptance criteria; a summary statement on the results; the hydraulic jack pressure gauge and load cell calibration report; and material certification, including grout compressive strength tests (e.g., only 3-day results may be available) and steel mill certifications.
key_points: Submit a report for each load test to the Owner, typically within 24 to 48 hours
Project description; site and subsurface conditions at the test location compared with those encountered
Key personnel: drill rig operator, superintendent, grout plant operator and others
Installation data: cased and uncased lengths, bags of cement, casing and reinforcement, geology, drilling and grouting records
Results with data sheets and figures; requirements, acceptance criteria and comparison; summary statement
Jack gauge and load cell calibration report; grout strength (maybe only 3-day) and steel mill certifications

sections.summary: Project load testing requirements are treated under 7.6.1 Introduction through 7.6.5 Method of Load Application; no text is printed under this heading.

sections.applicability: Pointer to planning the project load testing program (7.6.1 to 7.6.5).

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Scope the load testing program in design from: number of production micropiles; magnitude and type of design loading; sensitivity and importance of the structure; variability and types of subsurface conditions; access and headroom constraints; contractor experience. The specification should set the number and location of verification tests, number of proof tests, test load magnitudes, method of load application, load durations and acceptance criteria for maximum total and creep displacement.
sections.body: (p. 7-20) During design, consideration should be given to the scope of the micropile load testing program. Factors: total number of production micropiles; magnitude and type of design loading (compression, tension and/or lateral); sensitivity and importance of the supported structure; variance in subsurface conditions across the site; types of subsurface conditions; site access and headroom/installation constraints; and contractor experience. The project specification should include requirements for: the number and location of pre-production verification load tests; the number of production pile proof load tests; the magnitude of the test loads; the method of load application (single versus multiple cycles, order of testing); the duration for which test loads are applied; and acceptance criteria for maximum total displacement and maximum creep displacement at a specified load.
key_points: Scope factors: number of production micropiles, load type and magnitude, structure importance, ground variability and type, access and headroom, contractor experience
Specify number and location of verification tests and number of proof tests
Specify test load magnitudes, method of load application (cycles, order), load durations
Specify acceptance criteria for maximum total and maximum creep displacement at a specified load
sections.applicability: Factors that set the scope of a micropile load testing program and what the specification must require.

sections.title: Load Testing Program for Verification Tests
sections.summary: At least one pre-production verification test is required on all projects, to at least 2.0 times the design load per Table 7-1, on a sacrificial or production pile; loading further may seek the ultimate capacity. Planning: test near borings; review critical load combinations (tension or lateral tests in seismic regions; tension may substitute for compression, but if compression is critical at least one compression test); identify bond zone strata and weak or compressible horizons; test each significantly different stratum; consider access and schedule.
sections.body: (pp. 7-20 to 7-21) At least one pre-production verification micropile load test is required on all projects, performed to at least 2.0 times the design load in accordance with Table 7-1; it may be a sacrificial (non-production) or a production pile, and loading beyond the required minimum may be conducted to determine the ultimate capacity. Developing the program: prepare a site map of all proposed structures (e.g., pile caps) and boring locations, and test close to a boring so results can be correlated with stratigraphy; review the critical load combinations for each substructure unit to identify the types of test (in highly seismic regions tension and/or lateral tests may be required; tension tests may substitute for compression tests, but if compression loading is critical at least one verification test should be in compression); review all subsurface information to identify the strata where bond zones will form at each structure, including overall variability, and identify all soil/rock support horizons that may be relatively weak or compressible, since micropiles are often used in mixed ground; select the total number of tests so that at least one is performed in each significantly different support stratum, considering access and construction schedule, and where access to a location is difficult consider whether appropriate information can be obtained where access is better.
key_points: At least one verification test on every project, to at least 2.0 times the design load per Table 7-1
The verification pile may be sacrificial or a production pile; loading further may find the ultimate capacity
Locate tests close to borings to correlate results with stratigraphy
Seismic regions may need tension and/or lateral tests; if compression is critical, at least one verification test in compression
Identify bond zone strata and weak or compressible horizons in mixed ground
At least one verification test in each significantly different support stratum, considering access and schedule
sections.applicability: Minimum verification testing and how to plan the number and location of verification tests.

sections.title: Load Testing Program for Proof Tests
sections.summary: Proof tests confirm the contractor's procedures throughout the project; the Owner should give the number to be tested early and keep the right to add or relocate tests. Tension tests are usually cheaper (the ground gives the reaction), so proof tests may be tension only if tension is critical or correlates with the verification results. Testing 5 percent of production micropiles is a common rule of thumb that may not suit all applications; Table 7-3 gives minimum proof test frequencies.
sections.body: (pp. 7-21 to 7-22) Proof tests are performed primarily to confirm the contractor's construction procedures throughout the project. The Owner should provide the same information as for verification testing and give the Contractor the number of micropiles to be proof tested as early as possible during construction; the specifications should let the Owner request additional proof tests and relocate them for unacceptable results or varying ground. Proof testing may consist of compression and/or tension tests; tension tests are typically less expensive because the ground can provide the reaction instead of adjacent piles or tie-down anchors, so if the critical load condition is tension, or if production tension test results can be correlated with the pre-production tension and compression results, proof tests may consist of only tension tests. A common requirement is to test 5 percent of the production micropiles, similar to practice for driven piles for bridge foundations, but this 'rule of thumb' may not be appropriate for all applications; the recommendations in Table 7-3 should be used to evaluate minimum proof testing requirements.
key_points: Proof tests confirm construction procedures throughout the project
Owner states the number of proof tests early and may add or relocate tests for poor results or varying ground
Tension tests are usually cheaper (ground provides the reaction); proof tests may be tension only if tension is critical or results correlate
Testing 5 percent of production micropiles is a common rule of thumb that may not suit all applications
Table 7-3: underpinning and seismic retrofit, 1 proof test per substructure unit
Table 7-3: new construction, 1 per substructure unit but not less than 5 percent of production micropiles
Table 7-3: slope stabilization, 2 percent of production micropiles to a test load of 2.0 times Pult (Eq. 6-1)
tables: Table 7-3: Recommendations on Minimum Number of Test Micropiles for Proof Testing: underpinning applications, 1 micropile proof test per substructure unit; seismic retrofit, 1 micropile proof test per substructure unit; structural support of new construction, 1 micropile proof test per substructure unit but not less than 5 percent of total production micropiles; slope stabilization, 2 percent of total production micropiles to a test load of 2.0 times Pult (Pult defined in Eq. 6-1 in Chapter 6) (p. 7-22)
sections.applicability: Number and type of proof tests, with the minimum frequencies of Table 7-3.

sections.title: Test Load Magnitude
sections.summary: The test load is typically set by the desired geotechnical factor of safety, usually greater than the factor applied to ultimate structural capacity, so excess structural capacity may be needed to carry the test loads. For structural support applications the manual recommends verification tests to 2.0 x design load and proof tests to 1.6 x design load. Whether test pile reinforcement may be varied should be addressed in the specifications (see Chapter 5).
sections.body: (pp. 7-22 to 7-23) The test load magnitude is typically controlled by the desired geotechnical factor of safety, which is usually greater than the factors of safety applied for ultimate structural capacity, so excess structural capacity may be required for the micropile to support the test loads. For structural support applications this manual recommends: verification load testing to 2.0 x design load; proof load testing to 1.6 x design load. The geotechnical capacity of a micropile can affect the ultimate structural capacity, requiring the same factor of safety for both geotechnical and structural considerations. Whether the reinforcement can be varied for the test piles should be considered carefully and addressed in the project specifications; this issue is reviewed in Chapter 5.
key_points: Test load is set by the desired geotechnical factor of safety, usually greater than the structural one
Excess structural capacity may be needed for the test micropile to carry the test load
Structural support: verification tests to 2.0 x design load; proof tests to 1.6 x design load
Whether test pile reinforcement may differ should be addressed in the specifications (Chapter 5)
sections.applicability: Recommended verification and proof test loads for structural support micropiles.

sections.title: Method of Load Application
sections.summary: If micropiles carry tension and compression, test both; testing the same micropile in both, do tension first so the pile reseats in compression. All micropiles must be usable for proof testing since proof tests are random. Testing an inclined micropile is usually unnecessary: inclination has little effect on construction or capacity (particularly cased-hole micropiles) but makes testing harder and costlier. Slope stabilization micropiles may be tested in tension.
sections.body: (p. 7-23) If micropiles are designed for tension and compression loads, both conditions should be tested. If the same micropile is tested in both, the tension test should be conducted first, allowing the pile to be reseated during compression testing if some net upward residual movement occurs. Because proof tests are performed on random micropiles, the Contractor shall assure that all micropiles can be used for load testing. It is usually not necessary to test an inclined micropile even if the project includes them: installing on an incline has little, if any, effect on difficulty of construction and capacity, particularly for micropiles installed by the cased hole method, while testing an inclined micropile can be difficult and costly, particularly in compression. For slope stabilization micropiles, tension tests may be used.
key_points: Test both tension and compression if the micropiles are designed for both
Same micropile in both: tension test first so the pile reseats in compression
Proof tests are random, so all micropiles must be testable
Testing inclined micropiles is usually unnecessary; inclination has little effect on capacity, especially for cased-hole micropiles
Slope stabilization micropiles may be load tested in tension
sections.applicability: Order of tension and compression testing and testing of inclined micropiles.

sections.title: Other Load Testing Techniques
sections.summary: Other load testing techniques are treated under 7.7.1 General, 7.7.2 Dynamic Load Testing and 7.7.3 Statnamic Load Testing; no text is printed under this heading.
sections.body: (p. 7-23) No text is printed under this heading; see 7.7.1 General, 7.7.2 Dynamic Load Testing and 7.7.3 Statnamic Load Testing.
key_points: Alternatives to static proof tests: dynamic (PDA) testing (7.7.2) and Statnamic testing (7.7.3)

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Micropile proof tests currently use the same equipment and procedures as verification tests: cheaper (lower loads, shorter tests) but with the same set-up, a large part of the cost. Driven pile proof testing often uses a pile driving analyzer (PDA) correlated with project static tests, rapid and inexpensive; Statnamic testing can serve similarly alongside static tests. Neither is used regularly for micropiles yet, but use may increase with experience.
sections.body: (pp. 7-23 to 7-24) In current practice, micropile proof testing uses the same equipment and procedures as verification testing; it is less expensive because of lower maximum test loads and less time, but the test set-up, a significant part of the cost, is the same. For driven piles, 'proof' tests typically include dynamic testing with a pile driver analyzer (PDA), correlated with project-specific load tests and used as a quality control measure; PDA testing is rapid and inexpensive compared with full-scale static load testing, so it gives an approximate static capacity for a relatively large number of production piles at low cost. Statnamic testing may similarly be used for quality control and assurance together with full-scale static tests. Neither method is used on a regular basis for micropiles at this time, but they may be used increasingly as experience is gained.
key_points: Micropile proof tests use the verification test set-up, a significant part of the cost
Driven piles often use PDA dynamic testing correlated with static tests for quality control
Statnamic testing may also be used with full-scale static tests
Neither is used regularly for micropiles yet; use may increase with experience
sections.applicability: Why dynamic and Statnamic tests are of interest for micropile proof testing.

sections.title: Dynamic Load Testing
sections.summary: PDA testing needs a mobilized pile hammer; CAPWAP methods are in FHWA-HI-97-014. In Northern Virginia, Gomez et al. (2004) found two of three static tests in karst could not reach twice the design load (contaminated, poorly flushed bond zone); PDA on 22 production micropiles, with rising hammer energy and a field cushion, matched the static tests (Figure 7-12). Drawbacks: no creep, tension or lateral tests; risk of structural damage from eccentric hammer blows; expert interpretation; rarely cheaper than tension tests.
sections.body: (pp. 7-24 to 7-25) Although not commonplace, PDA testing for micropile proof testing could offer the same advantages as for driven piles; since micropiles are not driven, a pile hammer must be mobilized. Details of the PDA and CAPWAP data interpretation are in FHWA-HI-97-014 (1996). There is not yet sufficient field experience to develop general procedures, but one case history is reviewed. On a recent Northern Virginia project, Gomez et al. (2004) used PDA to evaluate micropiles installed through karstic limestone to competent rock (Figure 7-12). Static load tests on two of three test micropiles could not reach the test loads (two times the design load); the causes were contamination of the grout-rock contact in the bond zone and difficulty cleaning the bond zone by flushing with water. The capacity of production micropiles already installed then had to be evaluated, and PDA testing was performed on 22 production micropiles of varying lengths. Because of their small cross section there was concern about structural damage from hammer strikes, while sufficient energy must be imparted to move the pile enough to estimate capacity; hammer energy was increased gradually and a cushioning system was fabricated in the field. PDA capacities were consistent with the three static load tests, and the authors concluded PDA could give reasonably accurate capacity estimates for the remaining production micropiles. PDA can give cost advantages over static compression proof tests (many tests per day), but: the creep test cannot be performed; tension and lateral tests cannot be performed; potential structural damage, especially from eccentric hammer loading, must be considered; data interpretation must be by an engineer with detailed knowledge of the method; and where tension tests suffice to evaluate bond zone capacity, PDA is unlikely to be more cost-effective (unless test loads are very high, needing substantial reaction beams).
key_points: PDA testing of micropiles needs a mobilized pile hammer; PDA and CAPWAP details in FHWA-HI-97-014
Not enough field experience yet for general procedures
Gomez et al. (2004), Northern Virginia karst: two of three static tests failed to reach twice the design load (contaminated, poorly flushed bond zone)
PDA on 22 production micropiles with gradually increased hammer energy and a field-made cushion matched the static tests (Figure 7-12)
PDA cannot perform creep, tension or lateral tests
Risk of structural damage from eccentric hammer loading; interpretation needs an engineer who knows the method
Where tension tests suffice, PDA is unlikely to be cheaper unless test loads are very high

sections.title: Statnamic Load Testing
sections.summary: Statnamic testing (Bermingham and Jane, 1989 in the text) burns solid fuel in a pressure chamber to accelerate a reaction mass upward, pushing the pile down, then vents. It needs a level area 3 to 4 m across and at least 8.5 m headroom (Figure 7-13). Advantages: no reaction piles, quicker set-up, about one quarter to one half the cost of a static test, suits lateral, battered and over-water tests, simpler analysis. Disadvantages: no creep test, no tension tests yet, tight access, expert interpretation.
sections.body: (pp. 7-26 to 7-27) The Statnamic method was developed by Bermingham and Jane (1989) (listed in the references as Bermingham and James) and is used to evaluate the capacity of drilled shafts, driven piles, augered cast-in-place piles, micropiles, stone columns and shallow foundations; its use for micropiles is increasing and several projects have been completed, though data are unpublished. Equipment, testing methods and data interpretation are in Mullins et al. (2001). Solid fuel burned within a pressure chamber rapidly accelerates the reaction mass on the pile head upward, with an equal and opposite force pushing down on the pile; loading rises to a maximum and unloads by venting the gas. The magnitude and duration of load and the loading rate are controlled by the piston and cylinder size, fuel mass and type, reaction mass and venting technique. The work area must typically be 3 to 4 m (10 to 13 ft) in diameter and level (Figure 7-13), with at least 8.5 m (28 ft) of headroom. Advantages: no reaction piles or reaction system and less preparation time than a static test; cost on the order of one quarter to one half that of an equivalent static load test, depending on load, site and labor; readily adapted to lateral tests, batter micropiles and axial tests on land or over water; and a load duration long enough to preclude stress wave formation, so the analysis is simpler than for dynamic tests. Disadvantages: the creep test cannot be performed; tension tests have not yet been performed with the device; it may not suit tight access unless the test pile can be relocated; and interpretation must be by an engineer with detailed knowledge of the method and current analysis methods.
key_points: Statnamic: solid fuel in a pressure chamber accelerates a reaction mass upward, pushing the pile down; unloads by venting gas
Load magnitude, duration and rate set by piston and cylinder size, fuel mass and type, reaction mass and venting
Needs a level work area 3 to 4 m (10 to 13 ft) across and at least 8.5 m (28 ft) headroom (Figure 7-13)
Advantages: no reaction system, quicker set-up, about one quarter to one half the cost of an equivalent static test
Suits lateral tests, batter micropiles and over-water tests; no stress waves, so simpler analysis than dynamic tests
Disadvantages: no creep test, no tension tests yet, may not suit tight access, needs expert interpretation
